after: Fixed-fractional sizing means every trade risks the same slice of the account, so no single loss can hurt more than you chose. The desk's range is 0.25% to 2%: small when the setup is B grade, the market is yellow or you are trading badly; larger when the setup is A+, the market is green and you are in sync. The number of shares is never a guess. Take the risk in dollars (account times risk %), divide by the distance from your entry to your stop, and round down. A $100,000 account at 1% risk with a $2 stop distance is $1,000 / $2 = 500 shares. Why a fixed fraction and not a fixed dollar amount: as the account grows the bets grow with it, and as it shrinks the bets shrink, which is what keeps a losing streak survivable. The math of recovery is the reason: a 10% drawdown needs an 11% gain to get back, 20% needs 25%, 50% needs 100%. That is why the desk cuts max position size in a drawdown, 20% normally, 10% after a 6% drawdown, 8% after 8%, 5% after 10%, and only earns the size back as the equity curve turns up. Size steps down, not just risk, because a drawdown usually means your read of the tape is off, and the fastest way to stop a spiral is to make every mistake cheaper. This is different from Kelly sizing (which bets a fraction computed from win rate and payoff) and from ATR sizing (which sets the stop from volatility); the desk sets the stop from the chart first and lets the stop set the size.

after: Five longs in one sector are not five trades, they are one big bet on that sector. Count correlated names as one position when you think about how much of the book is on one idea. That is a judgment, not a hard cap: sometimes concentration is exactly what you want, when the theme is the leader and the setups are valid, and sometimes you load up on several mean-reversion names at once because each one is a good trade on its own. The tools flag sector concentration at 40% and open risk at 10% of the account so you see it; you decide.
note: hard caps removed; 40% sector flag and 10% heat kept as the tool's guardrails, not rules

after: The point of correlation-adjusted exposure is honesty about what you actually own. If the semis roll over, five semiconductor longs all hit their stops on the same day, so your real risk is five times one stop, not five independent coin flips. That is why the desk counts names in one theme as one trade when it sizes the book. It is not a rule that forbids concentration. When a theme is leading the market and the charts are giving valid entries, concentrating in it is how the best years are made; the risk is handled by the stops and by trimming as the names extend, not by refusing to own more than one. The same goes for loading up on several mean-reversion trades at once when each one qualifies on its own. What it does mean: know the number. The portfolio heat tool adds up open risk (entry to stop, times shares, across every position) against a 10% ceiling, and flags any sector over 40% of the book, so a crowded bet is never a surprise. Exposure overall comes from the firm's Exposure Rating, which sets how much of the account should be at work in that market; the correlation check is about how that exposure is spread. Ask three questions before adding a name: does it move with what I already own, what happens to the whole group if the sector gaps down, and is the setup good enough to deserve the crowding. If the answers are yes, yes and yes, take it and manage it.
